h1: Working in beer sales: what the job involves
title: Working in Beer Sales | Craft Beer School
desc: What a beer sales job involves day to day: accounts, tastings, orders, distributors, data and the skills that get you hired.
teaser: Beer sales is more than pouring samples. It is relationships, numbers and careful timing.
standfirst: Selling beer means helping bars, shops and distributors make money from your product. This guide explains the work and the skills behind it.
sections:
A small brewery's owner often does the selling. As it grows, it hires a sales representative or an account manager. Distributors have large teams that sell many brands at once. Importers, bottle shops and large retailers have buyers who choose what to stock. Every one of these roles needs someone who can talk to customers.

The structure differs by country. In some, breweries sell to a distributor by law before a beer reaches a shop. In others they sell directly. Learn the rules for your market.

Even a bar manager who orders weekly is making a sales decision. Treat that person as a customer you serve, not as an obstacle.

You visit outlets, take orders, check stock and deliver samples. You taste the range with buyers and answer questions about styles. You agree prices, promotions and delivery dates. You follow up on late payments and complaints. A good representative also notices what is not selling and asks why.

Paperwork is part of the job: order forms, invoices, delivery notes and records that alcohol rules require. Rules differ by country and change, so ask your employer for current guidance.

Weekends belong to events. Tastings, festivals and brewery nights are where the representative is most visible, so build rest into the week around them.

Buyers trust a representative who can explain a beer simply and honestly. Learn your styles, the ingredients and what to say about freshness and storage. Know how to tell a customer to keep hoppy beer cold. Read the beer styles guide and how to taste beer to build a vocabulary.

Know your competitors' beers too. A customer will ask how yours differs from the one on the next tap.

A simple habit helps: after every visit, write one line about what the customer said. Over a season those lines become a map of what the market wants.

Sales is a number business. You need to understand margin, the price per litre or per case, delivery cost and how much stock a bar can hold. A bar that has to throw away old beer will not reorder. Teach customers to rotate stock. Track which outlets sell through quickly.

Spreadsheets and customer records keep you organised. Digital tools help you plan visits and forecast demand. Brewery Business Management covers pricing, margin and planning in more depth than a job alone does.

A simple example: a bar that buys a keg for a price, sells every glass and throws away the last litre has a lower margin than the price list suggests. Ask about waste. Offer smaller kegs or a faster-selling style.

Listening beats talking. Ask what the bar's customers want, what space the cooler has and what they pay for similar beers. Follow up as promised. Turn up on time. Admit what you do not know and find out.

Responsible service is part of the job. Never encourage heavy drinking, never sell to anyone underage and follow local licensing law.

Remember names and small details, such as a manager's preference for dry beers or a chef's interest in seasonal food. People buy from those who remember them.

Representatives move to key account management, regional sales management, marketing or brand roles. Some set up their own distribution. A representative who understands production often becomes a valuable bridge between the brewhouse and the market.

See careers in non-alcoholic and low-alcohol drinks and from homebrewer to assistant brewer for other paths.

Distributors value reps who bring data, not just enthusiasm. Share sell-through figures and ask for theirs in return.

Work a taproom or bottle shop shift to learn the customer. Offer to help a brewery at a market stall. Learn the basics of how beer is made and priced. We do not quote salaries, since pay differs widely by country and company.

If you want to understand the commercial side from the brewery's point of view, our business management course covers costs, pricing and planning.

Reading reviews of your own beers is useful too. Customers often tell you what is wrong before the buyer does.
faqs: Do I need to know how to brew to sell beer?
No, but you must know the beer and be able to explain it. Some brewing knowledge builds trust.
Is beer sales a stable career?
It depends on the company and the market. Skills in relationships and numbers transfer to other drinks and goods.
Alcohol sales and shipping rules differ by country. Check your regulator.
What is the hardest part of the job?
Keeping accounts happy while managing stock, price and timing.
